title: Why You Should Limit Your Contact With Difficult Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that letting a written classroom management plan, rather than the teacher personally, absorb the burden of enforcement is especially powerful with difficult students, because it removes the teacher as a target of blame and forces students to confront their own responsibility for the first time. His central mechanism is that consistent, impersonal, referee-like enforcement leaves a student with no one else to blame -- not the teacher, not circumstance -- so the truth of their own choice eventually becomes unavoidable, similar to owning a driving mistake. He describes the personal payoff of this approach through an anecdote about difficult students voluntarily calling him 'sir' out of respect earned by the system rather than by personal charm, and closes by reiterating that the teacher's job is limited to great lessons, kindness, and consistent enforcement, while behavior itself belongs entirely to students.
points: Following the classroom management plan removes the teacher as a target of blame, forcing even difficult students to eventually own their own choices.
Consistent, exacting, referee-like enforcement applied identically to every student closes off a misbehaving student's ability to blame the teacher or circumstance.
The approach is described as especially effective with difficult students specifically because it strips away every excuse and external target for blame.
The teacher's responsibility is limited to great lessons, consistent kindness, and following the plan; listening, behaving, and learning remain entirely the students' responsibility.
quotes: It’s also a lot more effective than trying to convince, remind, persuade, intimidate, appease, flatter, lecture, reward, counsel, manipulate, or falsely praise students into behaving.

It does this this because it removes YOU from the accountability equation. You see, when there is no one to blame or rail against, your most challenging students naturally begin to point the finger at themselves.
It’s like backing a car into a light pole. It’s not the pole’s fault. It’s not the car’s fault.
My most challenging students call me sir. Every one of them. I’ve never asked them to.

And it’s that weight that transforms, that opens their eyes, that enables them to stand on their own two feet, accept both credit and blame, and become the mature, contented, and respectful students we want them to be.
